I think it's worth noting that the mainline RPG Maker series hasn't transitioned to Unity, and that Unite is its own standalone spin-off in line with the likes of the console spin-offs. So I wouldn't get too worried on that front!
Also the Makers being built on existing frameworks is nothing new--with even RPG Maker MV and MZ being built with the NW.js framework if I recall correctly. I think Unite was just poorly implemented and required a lot of outside hoops to be jumped like installing a Unity environment and having a Unity account and such. Godot is a bit more lax with those requirements and can probably have something far more integrated for the Action Game Maker more in line with traditional makers.
Whether the new mainline RPG Maker follows is yet to be seen, but given how often we usually see new RPG Makers I'm sure we'll hear something either this year or next about it.

posts.author: Slaughty
posts.body:
As someone who bought Pixel Game Maker early on, it was released too soon and with no real community to really support it like rpg maker has/had with Komodo/Degica. The built in tutorial for platformers had an infinite jumping bug, never fully localized tutorials, etc. That is probably the biggest problem Gotcha Gotcha games has at the moment. The RPG maker community has always filled in the gaps, provided tutorials, features that should be present from the get go, support and bug fixes. Clear example is Unite.
I will say using Godot as the backbone is better than Cuscos or whatever pixel game maker used and since Godot seems to have stopped the visual scripting support, it's a welcome addition, but it just seems like at that point, just learn Godot. Since the unity fiasco, there are way better tutorials and community support for Godot than there was a few years ago.

posts.author: MikePjr
posts.body:
As someone who's been using Pixel Game Maker MV (that's why i'm hardly on this forum anymore, gave up on RPG Making)
This successor should kick a lot of butt.
I been being super creative with PGM, and having a lot of fun with it.. the kind of fun i used to have with RPG Maker when i first discovered it way back in the early 2000s
I know people hate when a maker software isn't it's own software and gets built on something.. but this removes a lot of work needed by the developers.
If they started from scratch it would take forever.
Just take solace in knowing that GODOT is open source, unlike Unity.. we shouldn't see the issues we seen with "Unite".
I'd also encourage more folks here to give AGM a chance when it comes out.. especially if you have used PGM.. but even more especially if you haven't given these makers a shot and only been doing RPG Making.
-EDIT-
By the way, even though PGM started without much of a community, it has a thriving one now.
I'm one of them, i've even done tutorials, and i look forward to making tutorials for AGM as well.

I, for one, will not stand for this! I demand GGG make more archaic engines designed for making FF clones. We, the people, demand more RPG Maker shovelware with a new coat of paint!

To be honest, I really think anyone feeling excited about this should cool their jets.
And anyone suggesting that it will be cheaper than $80 should also probably cool their jets.
I believe the non-sale price of MZ is $80. Unite was around that price too. Inflatation is a thing, and the world's economy is a lot worse off than it was 4 years ago when MZ launched.
After such a spectacular disaster that was Unite, I would hold reservations on anything produced by GGG going forward; until they can prove to us (again) that they are still capable of making a functioning engine, there should only be reservations about whatever future product they release; otherwise your excitement is just feeding their marketing machine and may only lead to disappointment on your part.
As people have already mentioned, with it being Godot, it may just be more practical to download Godot (for free, by the way) and download an RPG/2D sidescroller framework.
This may just be grasping at straws on GGG part in order to recoup costs (and goodwill) that were burned from Unite.
Call me a cynic, but wake the f/ck up Samurai, we got corpos to burn.

posts.author: MikePjr
posts.body:
I've been using PGM going on 4 years, and if AGM is anything like PGM but improved, it'll be worth it.
But lord forbid a company try making a profit and people want paid for working on something.
I paid a discount for PGM, and after using it i feel like it would have been worth the full price had i known more about it at the time.. but at the time they had a lot to prove with PGM, and i feel like they've proven the concept and editor and so forth to me, and where PGM lacks, i'm certain that AGM will excel.
PGM was lacking a lot of things like visual effects, and layer options.. it was hard as hell to just replicate SNES like features, multi-panning layer sections.. it had to be faked with GIANT "objects" (PGM's version of Events) for like say.. clouds.. in the background.. or particles.
It also lacked things like distortion effects for scenes.. think SNES stages that are either under water or in very hot places..
But where PGM couldn't do that, GODOT alone can do those things, so i expect to be able to pull those things off in AGM.
I'm not a programmer, and i'll never be a programmer.. i'm an artist first and foremost.. so i NEED tools like GGG is selling.
And yes, i've tried the editor plugins and such for GODOT.. and i couldn't for the life of me wrap my brain around them.
If AGM is anything like PGM, i'll grasp it pretty easily.
My original comment asking people to try it had more to do with the fact that no one from the RPG Maker community jumped on board.. so PGM had to build it's own user base.. and it would have been nice to see more folks give it a chance.. but at the time of PGM's release.. unless i'm mistaken, we weren't allowed to talk about other makers amongst RPG Maker users.. so the exposure just wasn't there.
